title: Symbols, Holidays and Being a Citizen
bigQuestion: What do we share as a country, and what is my job in it?

story.title: The Class Pet Gets a Name
story.kicker: A new hamster needs a name. Twenty-two kids have ideas. How will they choose?
paragraphs: Room 12 has a new class pet. It is a small brown hamster. It runs on its wheel. It stuffs seeds in its cheeks. Everyone loves it. But it has no name.
"I want Peanut!" says Jae. "No, Biscuit!" says Ana. "Rocket!" says Sam. Soon everyone is shouting. Ms. Ortiz raises her hand. The room gets quiet. "We will vote," she says.
Ms. Ortiz writes three names on the board: Peanut, Biscuit, Rocket. Each kid gets one slip of paper. Each kid writes one name. No peeking. The slips go in a jar.
Ms. Ortiz counts. Peanut gets six. Rocket gets seven. Biscuit gets nine. "Biscuit wins," she says. Jae wanted Peanut. But he shrugs. "That was fair," he says. "Hi, Biscuit."
story.think: Why was voting a fair way to pick the name? What else could the class have done?

lessons.title: Stars and Stripes
lessons.mainIdea: The flag has fifty stars for fifty states and thirteen stripes for the first thirteen states.
reading: Look at the *flag* of the United States. It is red, white and blue. It has stars and stripes. A flag is a *symbol*. A symbol is a thing that stands for something bigger.
Count the stars. There are fifty. Each star stands for one state. Illinois is one star. Our country has fifty states, so the flag has fifty stars.
Count the stripes. There are thirteen. Seven are red. Six are white. They stand for the first thirteen states. Those states started our country long ago.

words.d: a piece of cloth with colors and shapes that stands for a country
a thing that stands for something bigger

look.title: Count the Flag
look.cite: The flag of the United States
look.prompt: What does each star stand for? What do the stripes stand for?

check.q: How many stars are on the flag?
check.why: The flag has fifty stars. Each star is one state.

check.q: What do the thirteen stripes stand for?
check.why: The stripes stand for the first thirteen states that started our country.

check.q: What is a symbol?
choices: A thing that stands for something bigger
check.why: A symbol stands for something bigger. The flag stands for our country.

lessons.title: The Pledge Is a Promise
lessons.mainIdea: The Pledge of Allegiance is a promise to be loyal to our country.
reading: Many schools say the *Pledge* in the morning. Kids stand up. They face the flag. They put a hand on their heart. They say the words together.
A pledge is a promise. The Pledge says we will be *loyal* to our country. Loyal means you stick with something and care for it. It says our country is one country, all together.
The Pledge ends with "liberty and justice for all." Liberty means being free. Justice means being fair. For all means everyone. That is the promise.

words.d: a promise you say out loud
to stick with something and care for it

look.title: The Words of the Pledge
look.text: I pledge allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America, and to the Republic for which it stands, one Nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.
look.cite: The Pledge of Allegiance, as set in United States law
look.prompt: Find the words "liberty" and "justice." What do they mean?

check.q: What is a pledge?
check.why: A pledge is a promise. The Pledge is a promise to our country.

check.q: What does liberty mean?
check.why: Liberty means being free.

check.q: Who is the promise of justice for?
check.why: The Pledge says "justice for all." All means everyone.

lessons.title: The Bald Eagle
lessons.mainIdea: The bald eagle is a symbol of our country because it is strong and free.
reading: A big bird flies over a river. It has a white head. It has a yellow beak. Its wings are wide. It is a *bald eagle*. It is not really bald. Its head feathers are white.
Long ago, the leaders of our country picked the eagle as a symbol. The eagle is strong. It flies high and free. Eagles live only in North America. That made it a good pick.
Look for the eagle. It is on coins. It is on dollar bills. It is on the seal of the president. Bald eagles live in Illinois too. You can see them by the Mississippi River in winter.

words.d: a big bird with a white head that is a symbol of the United States

look.title: Look at a Quarter
look.text: Take out a quarter. Look at the back. On many quarters, an eagle spreads its wings. It has a strong beak and sharp claws. Now look at a one-dollar bill. Turn it over. There is the eagle again, holding a branch and arrows.
look.prompt: Why do you think the eagle is on our money?

check.q: Why is the bald eagle a symbol of our country?
check.why: The eagle is strong and flies high and free. Leaders picked it long ago.

check.q: Is a bald eagle really bald?
choices: Yes, it has no feathers on its head
No, its head feathers are white
Yes, it is bald all over
check.why: The eagle's head feathers are white. It only looks bald from far away.

check.q: Where can you find a picture of the eagle?
check.why: The eagle is on coins, dollar bills and the president's seal.

lessons.title: A Bell and a Statue
lessons.mainIdea: The Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty are symbols of freedom.
reading: In Philadelphia there is an old bell. It is big and made of metal. It has a crack. It is the *Liberty Bell*. Long ago, it rang for our new country. Today it does not ring. But people come to see it.
In New York there is a giant green *statue*. A statue is a figure made of metal or stone. This one is a woman. She holds a torch up high. She is the Statue of Liberty.
France gave the statue to our country as a gift. That was more than one hundred years ago. Ships full of people sailed past her. She was the first thing they saw. She stands for freedom.

words.d: a figure of a person or animal made of metal or stone
a cracked old bell in Philadelphia that is a symbol of freedom

look.title: The Torch
look.text: Look at the statue. She is taller than a tall building. She wears a crown with seven points. In one hand she holds a book. In the other hand she holds a torch high in the air. A torch is a light. Her torch says: come this way.
look.prompt: Why do you think she holds a light up high?

check.q: Where is the Liberty Bell?
check.why: The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia. People go there to see it.

check.q: What does the Statue of Liberty hold up high?
check.why: She holds a torch up high in one hand. A torch is a light.

check.q: Who gave the statue to our country?
check.why: France gave the statue as a gift more than one hundred years ago.

lessons.title: Days for Great Leaders
lessons.mainIdea: Some holidays remember people, like Martin Luther King Jr. and our presidents.
reading: A *holiday* is a special day. Some holidays remember a person. In January we have Martin Luther King Jr. Day. Dr. King worked so that all people would be treated fairly, no matter their skin color.
Dr. King gave speeches. He led marches. He did not fight with fists. He used words. He said all kids should be able to play and learn together. Many people listened.
In February we have Presidents' Day. It remembers George Washington, our first president. It remembers Abraham Lincoln too. Lincoln lived in Illinois. Both were born in February.

words.d: a special day that a lot of people share

look.title: A March
look.text: Look at the old photo. Thousands of people walk down a wide street. They carry signs. Some signs say "Jobs." Some say "Freedom." Dr. King walks in front. No one is fighting. They are walking together to ask for fair treatment.
look.prompt: What did the people want? How did they ask for it?

check.q: What did Dr. King work for?
check.why: Dr. King worked so all people would be treated fairly, no matter their skin color.

check.q: How did Dr. King ask for change?
check.why: He used words. He gave speeches and led marches.

check.q: Presidents' Day remembers which two presidents most?
check.why: Presidents' Day remembers George Washington and Abraham Lincoln. Both were born in February.

lessons.title: Days for Our Country
lessons.mainIdea: Independence Day is our country's birthday, and Veterans Day thanks people who served.
reading: On the Fourth of July we have *Independence Day*. It is our country's birthday. On July 4, 1776, our leaders signed a paper. It said we were our own country. That was about 250 years ago.
People wave flags. They have parades. They watch fireworks at night. In Chicago, boats fill the lake. Families have picnics. It is a big party for the whole country.
On November 11 we have Veterans Day. A *veteran* is a person who served in the military. That means the army, the navy and more. We say thank you to them. Some kids have a veteran in their family.

words.d: the Fourth of July, our country's birthday
a person who served in the military

look.title: Two Parades
look.text: Look at the first parade. It is July. It is hot. Kids wave small flags. A band plays. At night, fireworks boom. Look at the second parade. It is November. It is cold. Old men and women in uniforms walk slowly. People clap and say thank you.
look.prompt: Which parade is Independence Day? Which is Veterans Day? How do you know?

check.q: When is Independence Day?
check.why: Independence Day is the Fourth of July. It is our country's birthday.

check.q: What is a veteran?
choices: A person who served in the military
check.why: A veteran served in the army, navy or another part of the military.

check.q: What happened on July 4, 1776?
choices: Leaders signed a paper saying we were our own country
check.why: On that day, leaders signed a paper. It said we were our own country.

lessons.title: People Who Made a Difference
lessons.mainIdea: Lincoln, Tubman, Chavez and Addams each helped other people and made things fairer.
reading: Abraham Lincoln lived in Illinois. He became president. Back then, some people were held as *slaves*. A slave is a person who is owned by someone else and is not free. Lincoln worked to end slavery.
Harriet Tubman was a slave. She ran away to be free. Then she went back. Again and again. She led many other people to freedom. It was very dangerous.
Cesar Chavez helped farm workers get fair pay. Jane Addams opened a big house in Chicago. Poor families came there to learn and get help. Each of these people saw a problem and helped.

words.d: a person who is owned by someone else and is not free
treating people the right way, with everyone getting a chance

look.title: Jane Addams's House
look.text: Look at the big house on Halsted Street in Chicago. It is 1889. Kids play in a yard. Inside, a mom learns to read. A nurse checks a baby. A boy paints a picture. Jane Addams walks through, saying hello to everyone.
look.prompt: Who came to the house? How did it help them?

check.q: What did Abraham Lincoln work to end?
check.why: Lincoln was president. He worked to end slavery.

check.q: What did Harriet Tubman do after she got free?
choices: She went back to lead others to freedom
check.why: Tubman went back again and again to lead other people to freedom.

check.q: What did Jane Addams do in Chicago?
choices: She opened a house to help poor families
check.why: Jane Addams opened a big house where poor families could learn and get help.

lessons.title: Vote, Help, Speak Up
lessons.mainIdea: A good citizen votes, helps others and speaks up when something is wrong.
reading: A *citizen* is a member of a country or a community. You are a citizen of your class. A good citizen helps. Pick up trash. Share. Help a friend who fell.
A good citizen *votes*. To vote is to choose. Each person gets one vote. The choice with the most votes wins. Grown-ups vote for leaders. Room 12 voted for Biscuit.
A good citizen speaks up. If something is not fair, say so. Say it kindly. Say it clearly. Dr. King spoke up. Jane Addams spoke up. You can too.

words.d: a member of a country or a community
to choose, with each person getting one choice

look.title: The Playground Problem
look.text: Only the big kids get the swings at recess. The little kids never get a turn. Nia thinks that is not fair. She could stay quiet. She could yell at the big kids. Or she could tell the teacher and ask the class to make a rule.
look.prompt: What should Nia do? What would a good citizen do?

check.q: What does it mean to vote?
choices: To choose, one vote per person
check.why: To vote is to choose. Each person gets one vote. Most votes wins.

check.q: Something at school is not fair. What does a good citizen do?
check.why: A good citizen speaks up when something is wrong. Say it kindly and clearly.

check.q: Which one is being a good citizen?
choices: Picking up trash on the playground
check.why: A good citizen helps. Picking up trash helps everyone.

review.q: What does each star on the flag stand for?
review.why: The flag has fifty stars for fifty states.
A pledge is a promise. The Pledge is a promise to be loyal to our country.

review.q: Which bird is a symbol of our country?
review.why: The bald eagle is strong and free. It is on coins and dollar bills.

review.q: Which holiday is our country's birthday?
review.why: Independence Day is July 4. Our country began on July 4, 1776.
Abraham Lincoln lived in Illinois before he became president. Dr. King was not a president.

review.q: Room 12 picked a name by voting. Why was that fair?
review.why: Each kid got one vote. The name with the most votes won.
